extracted.intended_audience: Wikipedia editors, especially contributors to WikiProject Mathematics and authors/editors of mathematics articles
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for when, how, and where to include mathematical proofs or proof-sketches in Wikipedia articles, and when a proof merits its own article. Covers style, naming, scope, alternatives, and relevant Wikipedia policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and amount of proofs in articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Wikipedia articles are akin to survey articles: they should contain a mixture of introductory information, context, definitions, results, pictures, and some discussion of proofs. It is not necessary for a Wikipedia article to prove every fact that is mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include brief but significant proofs or proof sketches to support the article's survey and reference aims. Avoid turning articles into textbook- or monograph-style repositories of detailed proofs. Prefer providing pointers and citations to textbooks or advanced monographs for full details; include only selected proofs that make the article more useful as a reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to place a proof in its own article
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no firm guidelines, but a proof may be given a dedicated article only if the proof is 'significant as a proof', not merely routine; WP:NOTTEXTBOOK applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not create a separate proof article if the proof appears verbatim in a standard textbook — instead transwiki to Wikibooks/Wikiversity/ProofWiki. Do not present unpublished novel proofs (avoids WP:OR). Use WP:GNG and WP:SIZESPLIT to determine sufficiency and whether to split a proof into its own page; generally reserve separate pages for proofs only when there is sufficient independent content to warrant it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and facets of 'proof significance'
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures that may support a proof being significant enough for its own article include features of the result, external features of the proof, internal/technical features, mathematical/conceptual features, and social or historical features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these facets in AfD debates or inclusion decisions: (1) the result's interest or surprisingness; (2) external features such as unusually long/short or machine-assisted proofs; (3) internal technical features with implications (e.g., elementary vs constructive); (4) conceptual neatness, elegance, or unexpected ideas; (5) social/historical impact (controversy or influence). Use these as evidence but note they are not an exhaustive list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding textbook-style or routine proofs (WP:NOTTEXTBOOK / WP:OR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs that are textbook-like, routine, or verbatim from standard textbooks are not appropriate for Wikipedia; novel proofs not previously published violate WP:OR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proof can be found verbatim in standard textbooks, transwiki it to other Wikimedia projects (Wikibooks/Wikiversity/ProofWiki). Do not include original, unpublished proofs. If the proof is routine or elementary and lengthy, prefer citation and summary rather than full derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation style for proofs (Manual of Style — mathematics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should conform as closely as possible to Wikipedia:Manual of Style (mathematics): present proofs in conversational prose, as if given in a lecture at a blackboard; avoid unnecessary symbols and jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid heavy use of symbolic shorthand (∀, ∃) and jargon; avoid phrases like 'Clearly...' and 'Obviously...'. Replace lengthy calculations with summaries where helpful. Do not put 'Q.E.D.' at the end; instead mark the end by a section heading or the end of the article. Using the imperative (e.g., 'Let ABC be a triangle…') is normal and acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use (and cautions) for collapsible frames
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proof is not significant enough for its own article but long enough to interrupt article flow, it may be set off in a collapsed frame using Collapse top/bottom templates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The use of collapsible frames violates MOS:COLLAPSE and is discouraged; a better style is to use explanatory footnotes for short/abbreviated proofs or to omit long proofs and replace them with a citation to a good presentation. The page includes example Collapse template code, but editors should prefer footnotes/citations over collapsed full proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming conventions for proof articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Common practice has been to name proof-related pages with words like 'Proof of ...' or 'Proof that ...', or names tied to the proof such as 'Furstenberg's proof of the infinitude of primes'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using subpages ('/Proof' or '/Proofs') for permanent encyclopedia content because that violates WP:SP. Use descriptive titles rather than subpage labels; ensure names conform to article naming policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalized proofs and fully mechanized proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Wikipedia articles do not typically include fully formalized proofs as would be generated by systems like Metamath, except in articles specifically about formal proofs or formal deduction systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include fully formalized machine proofs in general-topic mathematical articles; limit such content to articles where the subject matter is formal proofs themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of accepted and less-accepted proof presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: The page lists several articles that demonstrate widely accepted ways of including and writing about proofs and also gives examples of less widely accepted presentations (e.g., two-column style or overly lengthy elementary derivations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the listed accepted articles as stylistic models (e.g., Countable set, Isosceles triangle theorem, Difference of two squares). Avoid two-column presentations and long elementary derivations presented in overly technical or non-prose formats; if an example in Wikipedia is poorly presented, consider rewriting to prose or moving content to another project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Wikibooks/Wikiversity for textbook-style treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: Wikibooks and other Wikimedia projects are suitable alternatives for textbook-style, extensive derivations or full textbook treatments of proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If content removed from Wikipedia is textbook-like, consider moving it to Wikibooks/Wikiversity. Editors who want to work on textbook-style treatments should collaborate on those projects rather than expanding Wikipedia articles into textbooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with core Wikipedia policies when including proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs and proof-related content must comply with Wikipedia policies such as WP:Neutral point of view, WP:Verifiability, WP:No original research, WP:NOTTEXTBOOK, WP:NOTPAPER, and Scientific citation guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure proofs are verifiable and cited to reliable sources; avoid original research or unpublished proofs; maintain neutral tone; follow scientific citation standards. Use these policy constraints to decide inclusion, scope, and presentation of proofs.
